settle/valley: Picture a valley: a long, even slope down to a narrow bottom. A ball walks down it, each step the learning rate, eta, times the slope.
settle/small: With a small rate, the ball creeps: after thirty steps it is still far from the bottom.
settle/big: With a big rate it races down. But this slope never flattens, so the steps never shrink, and at the bottom the ball bounces side to side forever.
settle/both: So start big, then lower the rate as the walk goes on: down the slope fast, then smaller and smaller bounces, until it settles.
settle/name: One whole walk, first step to last, is a run. Lowering the rate over a run is called decay: it decays, the way a sound fades.
settle/schedule: The rate planned for every step is the run's schedule: here, held high, then sloping down.
steps/rule: The classic schedule goes in steps: hold the rate, then multiply it by a factor, often zero point one or a half, every so many steps. It makes a staircase.
steps/he: In 2015, Kaiming Her and colleagues at Microsoft trained an image recognizer this way: zero point one, divided by ten at step thirty-two thousand, and again at forty-eight thousand.
steps/one: Say it starts at zero point one and drops every ten thousand steps. By step fifteen thousand, one drop has happened: zero point one times zero point one, or zero point zero one.
steps/two: By twenty-five thousand, two drops have, each one multiplying by zero point one again: zero point one times zero point one squared, zero point zero zero one.
steps/edge: The two slashes count the drops: t divided by ten thousand, with the remainder thrown away. At exactly step twenty thousand that is two: the drop there has happened.
linear/top: Linear decay slides the rate down in a straight line instead. It starts at the top rate, eta max: here, the largest rate the run uses.
linear/bottom: It ends at the bottom rate, eta min,
linear/T: T steps later, falling by the same amount every step.
linear/gap: Take zero point one down to zero point zero one over a thousand steps: the whole fall, the gap, is zero point zero nine.
linear/frac: At step four hundred, the run is zero point four of the way along, so the rate has fallen zero point four of the gap: zero point zero three six.
linear/lr: Take that from the top: zero point one minus zero point zero three six leaves zero point zero six four.
warmup/wall: The start has its own trouble. Far from the bottom, the walls are often steep, and the gradient is large.
warmup/fly: At the full rate, the first step flies past the bottom onto the far wall, higher and steeper still. The next is bigger again: the walk blows up.
warmup/ramp: So ramp the rate up instead: from zero, in a straight line, to eta max over the first k steps. That is warmup.
warmup/grow: The first steps stay small while the wall is steep, and by the time the ball reaches gentler ground, the rate has grown.
warmup/formula: At step t the rate is eta max times t over k. With eta max at zero point one and k a thousand, step two hundred and fifty is a quarter of the way: zero point zero two five.
warmup/hold: Once t reaches k, the rate holds at eta max: step fifteen hundred runs at the full zero point one.
warmup/goyal: In 2017, Priya Goyal and colleagues at Facebook needed a rate of three point two. Jumping to it from a low rate set the run back for good; ramping up in a straight line fixed it. They called it gradual warmup.
